https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide deck presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at its November 1, 2022 workshop, reporting progress on the district's "World Class for All" strategic plan, also branded "Project 2026 Blueprint / District School Troy." The plan's pillars are aligned to three core values - Collaboration, Deep Learning, and Focus - and the accountability framework holds the team to defined Objectives and Key Results across three color-coded pillars.

Green Pillar (Early Childhood to Career): Objectives include continuing to invest in high-quality early childhood education and advocating for universal preschool access for all three- and four-year-olds, plus expanding college and career pathways for middle and high school students through expanded career and technical education, computer science access, work-based learning, credentials, and college credit. Key Results updated October 2022 report record Early Childhood Enrollment of 483 - broken out as Tuition 271 (88% TSD), GSRP 80 (91% TSD), PreK 67 (100% TSD), and ECP 65 (100% TSD) - plus F&P (Fountas & Pinnell) preschool-impact data and a Kindergarten Transition Committee. Celebrations (June-November 2022) include Portrait of a Graduate work with Tony Wagner, an August Board session, and two October community sessions. Challenges include early-childhood capacity limits and preschool-access barriers. November 2022 recommendations include a January 11, 2023 Preschool Information Night, developing an early middle college partnership with LTU (Lawrence Technological University), and continued Portrait of a Graduate work.

Red Pillar (Equity and Well-Being): Objectives include funding whole-child investments and community/wraparound services such as afterschool programs, hiring more counselors, social workers, and school psychologists, and assessing facility upgrades. Reported actions include recruiting and hiring a new Supervisor of Equity and Inclusion, A.L.I.C.E. 2-day administrator training, deploying classroom safety buckets, and administrator safety "tabletop" exercises. Planned January-June 2023 work includes a Middle School Advisory Study Team, a Student Code of Conduct Review Team, expanding the District/TEA Professional Relations Committee, and a book study of "Culturally Responsive Teaching & The Brain," alongside district- and data-level teams and monthly staff topics.

Blue Pillar (Deep Learning): Objectives include creating and sustaining MTSS systems of support that deepen learning and empower student voice, improving technology access with quality training, and pursuing global best practices (NPDL, the 6 C's, learning partnerships). Key results include elementary Resource and Teacher Consultants trained in Math Recovery, elementary and middle school math pilots rooted in professional learning partnerships, development of student digital portfolios to document learning over time, elementary Media team curriculum using inquiry and maker-centered practices, and elementary MTSS benchmark-data monitoring. The document is a strategic-progress report and contains no dollar amounts, votes, or contract terms.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Board of Education presentation, "The Future of Science in Troy," delivered November 1, 2022, outlining a redesign of the district's high school science program to align with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). Beginning with the Class of 2027, the three required science credits shift to Biology (1 credit), one semester each of Chemistry and Physics, a new Earth Science semester, and a science elective. Chemistry, Physics, and Earth Science all move to single-semester required courses phased in through 2025-26.

What it is
A Troy School District Board presentation dated November 1, 2022 on the future of secondary science instruction, aligning course offerings to the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) and revising graduation requirements.

Graduation requirement change (starting Class of 2027)
- Current: 3 science credits - Intro to Biology (1); Chemistry/Active Chemistry/Physics/Intro Physics (1); science elective (1).
- New: 3 science credits - Life Science: Biology 1 year (1 credit); Physical Science: Chemistry 0.5 credit + Physics 0.5 credit; Earth Science 0.5 credit; science elective 0.5 credit.

Course shifts
- Chemistry: moves to a required one-semester course (currently piloting); "Chemistry 2" being developed; Active Chemistry discontinued in 2023-24. Partnered with Dr. Israel Touitou of MSU's CREATE for STEM Institute.
- Physics: shifts to a required one-semester course, piloting in 2023-24; "Physics 2" for advanced students (AP Physics C); Intro Physics discontinued in 2024-25.
- Earth Science: new required one-semester course; Troy teachers collaborating with other Oakland County districts; pilot 2023-24, formalized 2024-25.

Pathways
Sample four-year pathways include General, Physics-focused (to AP Physics C), and Biomedical (GBBE plus AP Biology).

Purpose
Informs the Board of the multi-year plan (2022-23 through 2025-26) to deliver a consistent, NGSS-aligned science curriculum with multiple student pathways.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A PowerPoint presentation titled "The Future of Science in Troy," delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on November 1, 2022, describing a multi-year redesign of secondary science aligned to the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). The NGSS framework cited spans Life Science (25 standards, Biology), Physical Sciences (24 standards, Chemistry and Physics), and Earth & Space Science (19 standards, Earth Science), with the stated goal of a guaranteed and viable curriculum offering a consistent foundation plus choice and varied pathways.

Graduation requirement change: The current reality requires 3 science credits - Intro to Biology (1 credit); one of Chemistry, Active Chemistry, Physics, or Introductory Physics (1 credit); and a science elective (1 credit). The new requirements, starting with the Class of 2027, keep 3 credits but restructure them: Life Science - Biology, 1 year (1 credit); Physical Science - 1 semester Chemistry (0.5) plus 1 semester Physics (0.5); Earth Science - 1 semester (0.5 credit); and a science elective - 1 semester (0.5 credit).

Student pathways: Sample four-year sequences include a General pathway (Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Earth Science, then an elective such as Forensics, Astronomy, or Environmental), a Physics-focused pathway (adding a second-semester Physics and AP Physics C), and a Biomedical pathway (adding GBBE for a year and AP Biology).

Course-by-course shifts: Chemistry moves to a required one-semester course, currently being piloted; teachers were involved throughout development, and the team partnered with Dr. Israel Touitou from the CREATE for STEM Institute at Michigan State University. A second-semester "Chemistry 2" is being developed for students pursuing higher-level chemistry (AP, Organic), and Active Chemistry will no longer be taught in 2023-24. Physics also shifts to a required one-semester course; the physics team is pre-piloting and working through the structure, with a formal pilot in 2023-24 and a "Physics 2" course (toward AP Physics C) for advanced students; Intro Physics will no longer be taught in 2024-25. Earth Science becomes a new required one-semester course - the district currently requires none of the Earth and Space Science standards - with a team of Troy teachers joining other Oakland County districts to develop it, a pilot planned for 2023-24, and formalization in 2024-25.

Implementation summary by year: Biology sees no change across 2022-23 through 2025-26. Chemistry pilots a one-semester class in 2022-23 (in Active and Chem 1) and develops "Chem 2," then teaches the one-semester course and finalizes "Chem 2" in 2023-24, with no change thereafter. Physics develops its one-semester course in 2022-23 while still teaching Intro Physics, pilots it and develops "Physics 2" in 2023-24, and teaches/finalizes in 2024-25. Earth Science is developed in 2022-23, finalized in 2023-24, and taught in 2024-25. The deck concludes with a "Next Steps" slide.

A slide presentation titled 'Project 2026 Blueprint,' presented to the Troy Board of Education as the district's November 2022-23 Accountability Plan. The framework aligns the district's 'World Class for All' pillars to three core values - Collaboration, Deep Learning, and Focus - and holds the team accountable through stated Objectives and Key Results for each pillar.

The Green Pillar, 'Early Childhood to Career,' sets objectives to continue investing in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool access for all three- and four-year-olds, and to expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students. The plan aims to broaden access to high-quality career and technical education and computer science, connect underrepresented students to in-demand careers in high-growth sectors, and build partnerships with higher education and employers so students can pursue work-based learning, earn credentials, and/or earn college credit. Reported key results and celebrations for June-November 2022 include record early childhood enrollment of 483 students, broken down as Tuition 271 (88% TSD residents), GSRP 80 (91% TSD), PreK 67 (100% TSD), and ECP 65 (100% TSD). The district advanced its 'Portrait of a Graduate' (POG) work with author and education expert Tony Wagner, including an August session with the Board of Education and two October community sessions, and validated POG's importance to post-secondary preparation. Data presented indicate that a preschool experience yields an ELA advantage sustained through fifth grade - children without preschool were two to three times more likely to be below grade level - while noting COVID increased the number of kindergartners arriving without preschool, reversing a four-year positive trend. Challenges cited include capacity limits, barriers to preschool access, and aligning Media/Maker Space work with Career Readiness. November 2022 recommendations include a January 11, 2023 Preschool Information Night for recruitment, prioritized Career Readiness messaging with administrators, teachers, and counselors, and developing a Lawrence Technological University (LTU) partnership for early middle college adoption.

The Red Pillar, 'Equity and Well-Being,' sets objectives to fund additional investments supporting the whole child - including community schools offering wraparound services such as afterschool programs, and hiring more counselors, social workers, and school psychologists - and to assess and act on facility upgrades for a world-class learning environment across all school communities. Key results include increasing social work and counseling support in all buildings, reviewing and monitoring student data, emphasizing adult learning in well-being and equity, recruiting and hiring a new Supervisor of Equity and Inclusion, conducting A.L.I.C.E. two-day administrator training, deploying classroom safety buckets, and running administrator safety 'tabletop' exercises. Planned January-June 2023 work includes a Middle School Advisory Study Team, a Student Code of Conduct Review Team, expansion of the District/TEA Professional Relations Committee, a book study of 'Culturally Responsive Teaching & The Brain,' ongoing data reviews with interventions in progress, monthly staff learning topics, and establishment of a district-level team to create a common system of support. The presentation served as a progress update on the district's strategic plan rather than an action item.

A memorandum dated November 30, 2022 from Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations in the Troy School District Operations Department (1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083), to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, providing bid-pricing analysis for RFP 9952. The memo supports award of the Site Improvements - Retention Pond Restoration projects at Athens High School, Smith Middle School, and Costello Elementary School.

Bids were opened November 18, 2022. Twelve bid invitations were emailed; during the bidding window the district confirmed five bidders two days before the deadline, but only two firms - Simone Contracting and Eagle Excavating - ultimately submitted. One bidder withdrew the evening before, citing newly awarded projects and lack of capacity; one could not meet the bid timeline; and one never responded. Carson notes the work is scheduled to commence upon award, with winter being the preferred season because the areas are designed to retain or transport water as part of the drainage system.

The submitted prices were: Simone base bid $394,300 with an Athens alternate of $129,500; Eagle base bid $983,000 with an Athens alternate of $359,000. To justify the large spread, Carson compared the figures to the district's 2022 Retention Pond RFP results. Simone had completed similar work the prior year at Troy High, the Transportation Center, and Leonard, on schedule and budget. A Board of Education workshop presentation from December 2022 describing the Troy School District's Middle School Math Curriculum and Program Review. The district reports that it has used its current core resource, Big Ideas Math, for almost ten years and has learned enough over that period to warrant a fresh review.

Instructional vision: The review is grounded in the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) framework. The presentation cites the eight effective mathematics teaching practices from NCTM's 'Principles to Actions: Ensuring Mathematical Success for All' (2014) and lists the eight Standards for Mathematical Practice: make sense of problems and persevere in solving them; reason abstractly and quantitatively; construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; model with mathematics; use appropriate tools strategically; attend to precision; look for and make use of structure; and look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

Process (2021-2022): The district assembled a curriculum-review team of classroom teachers, math specialists, and curriculum and instruction specialists. The team researched best instructional practices, reviewed state standards, examined district data trends to identify needs, created partnerships with experts, learning organizations, and local districts, compiled potential resources for pilot teachers, and built a curriculum-review matrix to evaluate options for alignment with the TSD strategic plan.

Resources under pilot: Two problem-based resources were selected for classroom piloting. The Connected Mathematics Program (CMP), developed by Michigan State University, embeds important mathematical ideas in the context of interesting, connected problems so that students, with teacher support, abstract powerful ideas, problem-solving strategies, and ways of thinking. Illustrative Mathematics (IM), published by Imagine Learning, is described as a problem-based IM 6-8 core curriculum rooted in content and practice standards, in which students learn by doing mathematics, solving problems in mathematical and real-world contexts and constructing arguments using precise language.

Pilot structure: Twelve teachers are piloting the two resources across all grade levels, in both regular and honors sections, and at all buildings. Support includes district-wide collaboration, classroom visits, out-of-district site visits, coaching, and learning beyond the school day. Specifically, teachers received 1.5 days of professional development with CMP facilitators plus two job-embedded coaching experiences, and 1.5 days of PD with IM facilitators plus one job-embedded coaching experience. To evaluate the pilots, the team gathers qualitative and quantitative student and teacher data on engagement, student performance, joy, and usability, using teacher and student surveys administered twice during each pilot, along with assessments, classroom observations, student reflections, and classwork artifacts.

A board-governance self-evaluation template for the Troy School District Board of Education, covering the 2021-2022 school year. The instrument was developed from the concepts and language of Davis Campbell and Michael Fullan as set forth in their text 'The Governance Core: School Boards, Superintendents, and Schools Working Together,' with attribute wording pulled directly from the text where possible.

Purpose and method: The stated purpose is for trustees to reflect on their performance as a board and as individuals over the preceding twelve months and to use that introspection to develop concrete actions for improvement over the next twelve months. Each trustee assesses both the board as a whole and themselves on every attribute, focusing only on the past 12 months, using a four-point scale: 4 = 'a foundational strength of this board,' 3 = 'generally good,' 2 = 'needs improvement,' and 1 = 'a critical weakness of this board.' At the end of each section trustees give a summary or 'gestalt' rating (explicitly not required to be a mathematical average) and brainstorm one or two concrete, positive actions or procedural changes for improvement. Completed forms feed a constructive discussion at a board workshop.

Six key areas: The evaluation is organized around the six areas Campbell and Fullan identify as central to high-functioning boards: (1) Coherence - individuals' shared depth of understanding about the nature of the work; (2) Governance Mindset - core understanding of the basic principles of governance; (3) Strategic Focus; (4) Systems Thinking; (5) Deep Learning; and (6) Managing Manner. Each area carries a set of specific attributes.

Sample attributes: Under Coherence, the form lists items such as trustees having a depth of understanding about the work; demonstrating emotional commitment so the board 'owns' rather than 'observes' the strategic vision; reinforcing a culture of trust through reliability and competence; believing other trustees' motivations are honorable, ethical, and honest; maintaining confidentiality rules relating to personnel and closed-session content; interacting continuously to reconcile differences; recognizing the power of trustees working as a single board entity; reconciling personal core values with the board's shared moral imperative and strategic goals; avoiding representation of specific constituencies or single-issue agendas in favor of the district's systemwide purpose; remaining open to other trustees' priorities; showing willingness to compromise in service of the board's unity of purpose; abiding by board policy even when voting against a resolution and not undermining its implementation; avoiding intervening at the administrative level to solve constituents' problems; and believing the administration's motivations are honorable, ethical, and honest. A later section (Governance Mindset) opens with the board showing 'a unity of purpose driven by a shared moral imperative - a relentless commitment to the learning of all students, no exceptions.'

The document is a blank template (ratings and improvement ideas are left empty) intended to be completed by each trustee ahead of a board self-evaluation workshop.

This Operations Department memorandum, on Troy School District letterhead (1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083), is dated November 30, 2022 and runs from Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent - Business Services. It supports agenda item 8.A and provides bid pricing data for RFP 9952, the 2023 Site Improvements - Retention Pond Restoration projects at Athens High School, Smith Middle School, and Costello Elementary School. The work restores areas designed to retain or transport water as part of the district's drainage system, and winter is the preferred construction window.

On November 18, the district received two bids, from Simone Contracting and Eagle Excavating. Twelve bid invitations had been emailed; two days before the bid five bidders were confirmed, but the evening before, one withdrew citing newly awarded work and no remaining capacity, one could not meet the bid timeline, and one never responded. Simone's base bid was $394,300 with an Athens alternate of $129,500, while Eagle's base bid was $983,000 with an Athens alternate of $359,000 - a significant spread that prompted Carson to lay out comparison points.

Carson notes Simone completed similar work the prior year at Troy High, the Transportation Center, and Leonard, all per specification, on schedule and on budget, giving him confidence its price reflects the specified work. The Athens and Costello scopes had been part of the 2022 bid but were not awarded then due to budget availability. For Athens, 2022 bids ranged from $216K to $290K and Simone's 2023 bid is about $255K, roughly 10-15% above the low three bids from last year. For Costello, 2022 bids ranged from $101K to $173K and Simone's 2023 bid is about $151K, roughly 20-33% higher than last year's low three. Simone's combined Athens-and-Costello bid rose from $336K in 2022 to $406K in 2023, a difference of about 17%. Eagle's combined Athens-and-Costello bid rose from $423K to $1,025K, more than doubling year over year.

Based on this analysis, Carson concludes that Simone's bid is fair and reasonable relative to the prior year's bids - an increase of 15 to 30% is not unreasonable in the current market and economy - while Eagle's bid appears non-aggressive and likely reflects its current workload. The memo is one of several item-8.A documents supporting the Board's award of the retention-pond site work to Simone; companion documents include a bid summary spreadsheet, a board recommendation memo requesting a $421,901 award (including 7% contingency) from the Building and Site Sinking Fund, an owner's-representative recommendation letter from PEA and Associates, and the award resolution.

What it is
A resolution (agenda item 8.C) of the Troy School District Board of Education, County of Oakland, Michigan, authorizing '2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation),' considered at the December 13, 2022 regular meeting.

Voter authorization
- At the November 8, 2022 General School Election, voters approved issuing bonds, in one or more series, not to exceed $555,000,000 (the '2022 Bond Proposal').
- Purposes: remodeling/equipping/furnishing school buildings, athletic fields and playgrounds; erecting a replacement middle school and classroom and other additions; instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; acquiring and improving sites; and purchasing school buses.

This authorization (first series)
- Aggregate principal not to exceed $190,000,000.
- Denominations of $5,000; maturities on May 1 or November 1; final maturity within 30 years of issue.
- True interest cost not to exceed 6.50% per annum; underwriter's discount not to exceed 0.50%.
- May be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company (DTC).

Delegations
- Superintendent and Assistant Superintendent, Business Services (either acting individually, the 'Authorized Officer') may accept an underwriter's offer, negotiate and execute a bond purchase agreement, and approve related terms.

Set as agenda item 8.C for the December 13, 2022 regular meeting (7:00 p.m. local time), this is a resolution of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, titled 'Resolution Authorizing 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation).' The document is formatted for adoption, with blank PRESENT and ABSENT member lists and blanks for the members offering and supporting the preamble and resolution.

The resolution rests on voter authorization: at the General School Election held in the district on November 8, 2022, the qualified electors approved the issuance of bonds, in one or more series, in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000 - the '2022 Bond Proposal.' The approved purposes (the 'Projects') are remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom and other additions to existing school buildings and facilities; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; and acquiring, preparing, developing and improving sites, together with the purchase of school buses. Under Section 6, Article IX and Section 16, Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, the tax levies for these bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount.

This particular resolution authorizes the first series of bonds under the 2022 Bond Proposal, in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $190,000,000 (or a lesser amount as determined at sale), to pay a portion of the Projects' costs and the costs of issuance. The bonds are designated '2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation),' with name or suffix changes as appropriate for each series. Bond details: registered as to principal and interest in denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples; dated as of the delivery date or another date set by the Authorized Officer; maturing on May 1 or November 1 in years and amounts determined at sale, with final maturity no later than thirty (30) years from issuance. Interest is payable semi-annually on May 1 and November 1 at a rate or rates set upon negotiated sale, not exceeding a true interest cost of six and one-half percent (6.50%) per annum, with the underwriter's discount not to exceed 0.50% of principal. Principal is payable at a bank or trust company serving as registrar and transfer agent (the 'Transfer Agent'); interest is paid by check to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month before each payment date. The bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company in New York, and may be issued as serial or term bonds, subject to optional or mandatory redemption prior to maturity at times, manner and prices to be determined.

The resolution also authorizes the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services - either one acting individually as the 'Authorized Officer' - to accept an underwriter's offer to purchase the bonds, and to negotiate, approve and execute a bond purchase agreement and various related terms and documents for the sale and delivery of the bonds. Finally, it recognizes that the district must either be granted qualified status within the meaning of Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended (the 'Act'), or receive prior approval of the bonds from the Michigan Department of Treasury.

The agreement runs from 2022 through June 30, 2025. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A Letter of Understanding entered between the Consortium Districts and their respective Education Associations, setting terms and conditions of employment for teachers assigned to the International Academy. It was included in the December 13, 2022 Regular Meeting packet.

About the International Academy
- A consortium of public school districts pooling resources to run a grade 9-12 program operating as a school of choice for consortium residents, at various locations (Okma, East, and West campuses).
- Staff are employees of Bloomfield Hills Schools; teachers remain employees of their home school district and are assigned to the Academy.

Duration
- In effect from 2022 through June 30, 2025.

Key terms
- Selection/transfers/termination/RIF: teachers stay home-district employees; vacancies posted electronically to home districts; termination follows home-district CBA, policy, law, and the Michigan Teachers' Tenure Act.
- Wages: paid per home-district step and salary track on the home-district pay schedule.
- Stipends (Appendix A): for required days/hours beyond the home district's work year; for 2022-23 paid in two installments (first December payroll, last June payroll); from 2023-24 folded into regular salary.
- Also covers supplemental/club pay (Appendix B), department chairs, work-year/calendars (Appendix C), tenure, grievance and arbitration, teaching schedule, academic freedom, mentorship, and substitution pay.

Purpose
To amend and supplement each teacher's home-district collective bargaining agreement for the specific conditions of Academy assignment.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The International Academy Letter of Understanding is a multi-year employment agreement covering teachers assigned to the International Academy, presented within the Troy School District's December 13, 2022 Regular Meeting materials. It is entered between the Consortium Districts and the respective Education Associations for the purpose of establishing terms and conditions of employment for teachers employed by Bloomfield Hills Schools and assigned to the International Academy. The Academy is described as a consortium of public school districts that have combined resources to provide a grade nine through twelve program operating as a school of choice for residents of the consortium districts, operating at various locations across those districts.

Duration: The agreement is in effect from 2022 (specific start date left blank) through June 30, 2025.

Selection of Personnel, Transfers, Terminations and Reduction in Force: Teachers assigned to the Academy are employees of the home school district, not of the International Academy Consortium; a home district may hire a teacher for the purpose of assigning that teacher to the Academy. Staff are selected from qualified teacher applicants employed by the consortium districts, with the Academy's administration determining qualifications; if a position cannot be filled that way, the Academy asks a consortium district to hire a qualified candidate. Vacancies are provided electronically to home districts. Nothing prevents a home district from terminating a teacher under its own collective bargaining agreement, policies and procedures, applicable law, and/or the Michigan Teachers' Tenure Act.

Wage Issues: Payment for required days follows the appropriate step and salary track of the teacher's home district, with regular paychecks issued on the home-district pay schedule. For required days and hours worked beyond the home district's regular work year and day, teachers receive a stipend at rates set in Appendix A. For the 2022-2023 school year the stipend is paid in two installments (the first payroll in December and the last payroll in June); beginning in 2023-2024 the total stipend is paid as part of the teacher's regular salary, commensurate with the bargained number of pays in the home-district contract.

The table of contents shows the full scope: duration; selection/transfers/terminations/RIF; wage issues (including special compensation); supplemental activities and club pay; department chairs; work year for staff (with 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25 calendars in Appendix C, discretionary and student days, open house, parent/guardian/teacher conferences, guidance counselor, and professional development); tenure; grievance procedure (definitions, time limits, association representative, procedure, power of arbitrator, miscellaneous provisions); teaching schedule; academic freedom; a professional development committee; and other issues (teachers will not evaluate staff, school closing, leave days, absence reporting, compensation for substituting for another Academy teacher, compensation for conferences, mentorship program, teacher handbook, and a statement that the agreement does not establish precedent at consortium districts). Appendices include stipend rates (A), co- and extra-curricular pay (B), school calendars (C), daily schedules for the Okma, East, and West campuses (D), the International Academy guidance counselor (E), a department chair job description (F), and the mentor/mentee committee chair (G).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Supplemental documentation prepared for RFP 9951, the Troy High School stadium turf replacement project, explaining the reasoning behind the recommended bid awards ahead of board consideration. The memo describes a collaborative team assembled to weigh priorities and opportunities for the stadium turf replacement, consisting of Christine DiPilato, Remo Roncone, Tim Fulcher, Shane Hynes, Larry Franckowiak, Mark Paulus, and the author. Mike Sims of Foresite Design served as lead architect providing technical advice and general counsel, and Mark Paulus is described as an owner's representative with extensive project-management experience.

The RFP was written as a general specification to create a competitive, level bid environment in which multiple vendors could price the base work on an even footing, while each vendor was encouraged to submit voluntary alternates for enhanced next-generation systems unique to its manufacturing. Extensive proposal evaluations and virtual post-bid meetings were conducted with each turf-system manufacturer to assess bid thoroughness, accuracy, and alternate proposals, by Tim, Shane, Larry, Mark, Mike, and the author.

The group reported unanimous agreement on three decisions. First, removal and replacement of the existing E-layer beneath the turf via Alternate 'a' from S&H Trucking, on the reasoning that the existing E-layer is 20 years old and the risk of keeping it for another 12 years outweighs the savings. Second, installation of a new E-layer or shock pad under the D area via Alternate 'g' from Goddard Coatings, which offered a $50,000 deduct if the new pad is selected. Third, selection of Shaw Integrated and Turf Solutions' Alternate 'e', the Game On Hybrid 2.0 system.

The memo argues the Shaw Game On system represents the newest generation of turf technology based on 20 years of evaluation. While each manufacturer offers a similar hybrid system differentiated by material weight, infill mix, and tufting/seams, Shaw's Game On is described as the only manufacturer to offer three colors of tufting from the factory. This feature is said to allow the field to have 9-10 times fewer inlaid seams than any competing product, an advantage currently exclusive to the Shaw Game On system. Because inlaid seams are field-cut on site to install field lines, numbers, logos, and similar markings -- and, in the author's 20 years of experience with synthetic turf, are the highest-percentage source of warranty and repair issues -- the design would eliminate inlaid seams everywhere on the field except the center logo and lacrosse bearing points. The unanimous consensus was that the Shaw Game On turf system would provide the best playing surface, aesthetics, reliability, and a world-class field for the Troy High stadium, with Foresite Design agreeing that, if funding availability supports it, the group's recommendation would be preferred.

What it is
A supplemental explanatory document for RFP 9951, the Troy High School stadium synthetic turf replacement, laying out the reasoning behind the project team's turf-system recommendation for the January 17, 2023 board meeting.

Who was involved
- Collaborative team: Christine DiPilato, Remo Roncone, Tim Fulcher, Shane Hynes, Larry Franckowiak, Mark Paulus, and the author (Operations Director Rob Carson)
- Mike Sims of Foresite Design served as lead architect and technical advisor
- Mark Paulus is an owner's representative with project-management experience

Unanimous recommendations
- Remove and replace the existing E-layer under the turf (Alternate "a," S&H Trucking); the current E-layer is 20 years old and the risk outweighs the savings of keeping it another 12 years
- Install a new E-layer/shock pad under the "D" area (Alternate "G," Goddard Coatings), with a $50,000 deduct if the new pad is selected
- Adopt Shaw Integrated and Turf Solutions' GameOn Hybrid 2.0 system (Alternate "e")

Why GameOn
Shaw is the only manufacturer offering three colors of tufting from the factory, allowing roughly 9-10 times fewer inlaid seams. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Supplemental documentation supporting RFP 9951, the Troy High School stadium synthetic turf replacement project, prepared by the Troy School District Operations Department to explain the reasoning behind its turf-system recommendation. It accompanies the award memo, resolution, and consultant letter presented under agenda item 11.A at the January 17, 2023 Board of Education meeting.

The document explains that a collaborative team was created to discuss priorities and opportunities for the stadium turf replacement. The team consisted of Christine DiPilato, Remo Roncone, Tim Fulcher, Shane Hynes, Larry Franckowiak, Mark Paulus, and the author (Operations Director Rob Carson). Mike Sims of Foresite Design served as the lead architect, providing technical advice and general counsel, while Mark Paulus is described as an owner's representative with extensive project-management experience. The RFP was intentionally written as a general specification to create a competitive, even-playing-field bid environment, with vendors encouraged to submit voluntary alternates for enhanced, "next generation" systems unique to each manufacturer. Extensive evaluations and virtual post-bid meetings were held with each turf manufacturer to assess bid thoroughness, accuracy, and the alternate proposals.

The group reported unanimous agreement on the following decisions:

E-layer removal and replacement under the turf (Alternate "a," S&H Trucking): The existing E-layer is 20 years old, and the team judged the risk of keeping it another 12 years to be greater than the savings.

New E-layer or shock pad under the "D" area (Alternate "G," Goddard Coatings): The coating company offered a $50,000 deduct if the new pad is selected.

Turf system selection (Alternate "e," Shaw Integrated and Turf Solutions' GameOn Hybrid 2.0): This is characterized as the newest generation of turf technology based on 20 years of evaluation. While each manufacturer offers similar hybrid systems with unique features - material weight, infill mix, tufting and seams - Shaw's GameOn system is the only one to offer three colors of tufting from the factory. That feature allows the field to have roughly 9 to 10 times fewer inlaid seams than any other system, a capability the document describes as currently exclusive to Shaw's GameOn. Because inlaid seams are field-cut on site to install field lines, numbers, and logos, and (in the author's 20 years of experience with synthetic turf) are easily the highest source of warranty and repair issues, the GameOn system would eliminate inlaid seams everywhere on the field except the center logo and lacrosse bearing points.

The unanimous consensus was that the Shaw GameOn turf system would provide the best playing surface, aesthetics, reliability, and world-class turf for the Troy High stadium, and Foresite Design agrees that, if funding availability supports it, this would be the group's preferred recommendation.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The draft 'Resolution in Support of Stormwater Management Plan' of the Troy School District Board of Education (agenda item 4.K), prepared for adoption to accompany the district's municipal separate storm sewer system (MS4) discharge permit application.

The resolution opens with a series of WHEREAS recitals. It states that Troy School District owns and operates facilities within the boundaries of the 'Detroit' urbanized area which discharges stormwater through an MS4 to surface waters of the State of Michigan; that the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy maintains oversight and regulatory authority for compliance with the NPDES Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System discharge permit; that the district has applied for and received permit coverage to discharge stormwater from its facilities to the MS4; and that the district agrees to comply with the permit requirements. It further recites that the district has developed a Stormwater Management Program Plan (SWMP) outlining the policies, procedures, and best management practices to comply with the permit.

The recitals then enumerate the district's specific commitments: to develop policies and procedures that prohibit illicit discharges to the stormwater system and to implement enforcement procedures to detect and eliminate them; to prohibit the discharge of non-stormwater discharges into the storm drain system, including pollutants or waters containing any pollutants; to eliminate illicit discharges and illicit connections; and to prohibit the construction, use, maintenance, or continued existence of illicit connections to the storm drain system -- expressly including illicit connections made in the past, regardless of whether permissible under law or practices prevailing at the time of connection. The district also agrees to obtain a Part 91 permit from the appropriate state, county, or local soil-erosion permitting agency, and a construction site permit from the local municipality or governing unit, for new development and redevelopment projects that disturb one or more acres; to inspect, operate, and maintain structural controls to reduce pollutant contribution, control runoff, and decrease or eliminate streambank erosion due to stormwater runoff; and to comply with the State of Michigan Permit (Rule 323.2190) for stormwater discharge from construction activity.

The operative clause resolves that the Troy School District Board of Education is highly committed to practicing sound environmental principles, including the reduction of pollutants to surface waters through stormwater discharges. The Board approves and instructs the district Superintendent to enforce the listed policies and procedures for illicit discharge elimination, control of stormwater runoff, and long-term operation and maintenance of structural controls as part of the overall Troy School District Stormwater Management Program Plan. The resolution is to be duly passed and approved by the Board of Education, Oakland County, Michigan, on a blank-dated line, with approval and attest signature blocks for Karl Schmidt, President, and Gary Hauff, Secretary.

The motion carried 6 Yes, 0 No, with Gottlieb absent.

Item 22-088 concerned a Purchase Agreement for Section 1 Preservation. It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne. The resolution recited that on March 20, 2018 the Board had resolved that the School District property known as Section 1 be split into two parcels, so the front portion could be sold to a developer for residential purposes and the remaining portion preserved in perpetuity; that the District had negotiated an Agreement of Purchase and Sale for the sale and preservation of the remaining 69.51 +/- acres of Section 1 with Six Rivers Land Conservancy, a Michigan non-profit corporation whose mission is to 'conserve, sustain, and connect natural areas, lands, and waters that make the places we live special'; and that the District had reviewed the Agreement (already executed by Six Rivers and attached as Exhibit A) and wished to approve it on substantially similar terms and to authorize the Superintendent, or his designee, to execute it and all related documents. The resolution authorized the sale and preservation of the premises on those terms and empowered the Superintendent or designee to execute the Agreement, any extensions, and all other necessary documents. The resolution was declared adopted, attested by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary of the Board of Education.

The business agenda also listed item 22-089, the 2023 School Building and Site Bond Sale Authorizing Resolution (Series 1).
